To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there is no difference between normal and transforming cultures in the turnover of hyaluronic acids, glycoproteins and chondroitin polysaccharides and (2) there is no evidence to support the hypothesis that nonspecific degrada- tion of cell surface carbohydrates is involved in the process of malignant trans- formation.
the net turnover kinetics of cell surface hyaluronic acids, glycoproteins and chondroitin sulfates are not altered during the process of Rous sarcoma transformation.
the turnover of cell surface hyaluronic acids, glycoproteins and chondroitin sulfates is not altered during the process of Rous sarcoma viral transformation of chick embryo cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular mechanisms involved in the process of malignant cellular transformation.

the role of the carbohydrate components of glycoproteins and glycolipids as potential mediators in the interaction of cells with other cells and extracellular matrices, in the regulation of cell growth and differentiation, and in the process of malignant neoplastic transformation.
the study of the molecular basis of cancer and the development of new approaches to cancer chemotherapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no differences in the turnover of the major cell surface polysaccharides in normal and RSV-transformed cells.
the turnover of cell surface glycoproteins and glycolipids is not altered in RSV-transformed chick embryo fibroblast cultures.
the process of transformation by Rous sarcomavirus is not accompanied by any detectable alteration of the net turnover of the major glycoconjugates of chick embryo fibrolasts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cell surface is not altered in the process of malignant conversion.
the turnover of the major cell-surface glycoproteins is not altered during transformation.
there is no evidence for the involvement of the cell surface carbohydrates in transformation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while there are many differences between normal and transformed cells, there is no evidence that these differences involve alterations in cell surface glycosaminoglycan metabolism.
there is no evidence for a generalized change in the metabolism of cell surface glycosaminoglycans during transformation.
the turnover of cell surface carbohydrates in normal and transformed cells is not different.
